transcript_window.text: I wanted to get more people involved in this kind of technology.
So at the age of 20, he learned everything he needed to start his own internet service provider.
Yep, this was in my very first apartment on East 10th Street in the East Village in Manhattan.
And my apartment had an old no longer working fireplace that was wasted space because you could never fire in it.
And the chimney was plugged up.
But I filled that space with a bunch of modems.
I ended up getting something like eight modems and I had them all in there.
And like one server running Linux, which was like super new at that point.
name of the ISP was called Calix.
And now that he had it stood up, he had to go around and talk to people and convince them to be customers.
who I knew in New York City that were trying to do some type of either activism or social change or just trying to have some trying to create a social movement and things like that.
so I went around and I tried to convince them that this internet thing was gonna be huge and just like a paradigm -changing thing that they needed to find out about.
And I remember getting a lot of pushback from people who were like, no, that's not for us.
That's for them.
don't really want that.
And I literally just trying to get people to get email and domain names and just like put out a newsletter or put up a little web page, something.
And it was hard to convince people at the time.
It's crazy to think back then.
were not interested in spreading their message online.
But yeah, that was a time when the was very geeky and difficult to use.
And it was new to everyone.
So it made sense why people just weren't quite ready yet.
And he kept trying to sell internet access to others and finally got some customers near the end of 1994.
one of the first organizations that I got online was called the New York Civil Liberties Union, which is the New York branch of the ACLU.
And you know, were pretty prominent in New York.
You always heard about them on the news.
